title: Photon Correlation Spectroscopy as a Probe of Critical Fluctuations in Correlated Electron Systems
authors: Natasha Kiper, Bertrand Evrard, Yuya Shimazaki, Ido Schwartz, Martin Kroner, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Atac Imamoglu
abstract: Characterizing phase transitions between correlated electronic phases, extracting their critical exponents, and identifying their universality class are of central interest in many-body physics. Here, we propose and demonstrate that photon correlation spectroscopy can be used to gain insight into the nature of critical electronic density fluctuations. We study a semiconductor moiré material consisting of two MoSe2 layers separated by a monolayer h-BN spacer and measure interlayer electron dynamics via the second-order correlation function of the scattered photons. The correlated transfer of large numbers of electrons between the layers at the onset of an Ising-type layer pseudo-spin phase transition leads to photon bunching in light scattered by the exciton resonance of one layer. Our measurements pave the way for using photon correlations as a method to access dynamical exponents associated with electronic phase transitions.
summary: The paper proposes using photon correlation spectroscopy as a novel diagnostic tool to study phase transitions in correlated electron systems. By measuring photon bunching in a moiré TMD heterostructure, the authors successfully linked optical measurements to the underlying electronic density fluctuations associated with an Ising-type layer pseudo-spin transition. This paves the way for accessing dynamical critical exponents using light scattering.
main_problem: The central goal is characterizing phase transitions between correlated electronic phases by extracting critical exponents and identifying their universality class.
main_result: Photon correlation spectroscopy successfully demonstrated that photon bunching during an Ising-type layer pseudo-spin phase transition provides a measurable signature of underlying electronic density fluctuations.
method: The authors use Photon Correlation Spectroscopy (measuring the second-order autocorrelation function g^(2)(τ)) applied to light scattered from a moiré heterostructure.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a semiconductor moiré material made of two MoSe2 layers separated by an h-BN spacer, which exhibits layer polarization analogous to an Ising pseudo-spin system.
key_observables: Photon bunching (g^(2)(0) > 1), the correlation length ($\xi$), and characteristic decay time ($t_d$).
important_parameters: Applied electric field ($V_E$) controlling the layer polarization, and the degree of electron density fluctuation.
main_assumptions: The technique assumes that light scattering fluctuations are linearly proportional to instantaneous charge density fluctuations ($\delta D \propto \eta \cdot \delta n_e(t)$), and that exciton decay is fast compared to electronic timescales.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup, resonance fluorescence spectra, and comparisons of g^(2)(τ) measurements at different light powers, showing increased bunching near the transition point.
paper_structure: The paper introduces PCS as a diagnostic tool for critical fluctuations in correlated systems. It details the experimental realization using moiré TMDs, demonstrating that electron transfer during a phase transition manifests as measurable photon bunching, thus linking optical diagnostics to electronic criticality.
why_interesting: This work provides an entirely new, non-invasive optical probe (photon correlations) to study dynamical critical exponents in strongly correlated 2D materials, bridging quantum optics with condensed matter theory.
